# gba-emu: rules for every agent

Read PLAN.md before starting. It defines the phases, the shared contracts and who owns which file.
The benchmark lives at `/var/www/html/test-projects/gba-eval`, referred to below as `$GBA_EVAL`.
Use that absolute path; relative paths break inside worktrees.

## Originality (hard rule)
- Write all code yourself. Do not read, copy, or paraphrase any existing emulator:
  `$GBA_EVAL/candidates/` (gba-core), `$GBA_EVAL/third_party/` (Mesen2),
  `$GBA_EVAL/reference/mesen_step.cpp`, or mGBA/NanoBoyAdvance/VBA/etc. from memory or the web.
- Allowed sources: `$GBA_EVAL/spec/gbatek.htm` (GBA, ARM and THUMB chapters only), `$GBA_EVAL/spec/ABI.md`,
  `$GBA_EVAL/spec/gba_bios_stub.h`, the grader's outputs (scores, `.ref.png` vs `.cand.png`),
  and running ROMs from `$GBA_EVAL/corpus/roms/`.
- No per-ROM hacks: never branch on a ROM's hash, title, or game code. Fix the hardware behavior.

## Code readability
- Use clear, descriptive names for functions, variables and types: `destination_register`, `shift_amount`,
  `fn execute_data_processing`. Never cryptic ones like `x`, `t`, `rd2` or `tmp`. Loop indices
  (`i`, `line`) are fine when the meaning is obvious.
- Official gbatek register and field names are allowed (`DISPCNT`, `BG0CNT`, `IE`, `IF`, `CPSR`, `Rd`, `Rn`),
  each with a short plain-English comment where it is defined, e.g. `const DISPCNT: u32 = 0x000; // display control`.
- Every non-obvious function gets a one-line doc comment naming the gbatek section it implements, e.g.
  `/// Barrel shifter for data-processing operand 2 (gbatek: ARM Opcodes: Data Processing (ALU)).`
- Prefer small readable functions over clever one-liners. Split a long `match` arm or a dense bit-twiddling
  expression into a named helper.

## Ownership
- Only edit the files your task owns (see the ownership tables in PLAN.md).
- Shared files (`src/lib.rs`, `src/gba.rs`, `src/bus.rs`, `src/io.rs`, `src/irq.rs`, `src/scheduler.rs`,
  `Cargo.toml`) are changed only by the integrator (the executor session). If you need a contract
  change, say so in your report instead of making it.

## Git
- Remote: https://github.com/Rohan-Jalil/gba-eval-trial-rohan. Never push; the human pushes.
- Author and committer: Rohan Jalil <[REDACTED:email]>. This is set in this repo's git config;
  do not override it.
- Use Conventional Commits: `type(scope): summary`, for example `feat(cpu): add ARM data-processing ops`,
  `fix(ppu): wrap affine BG coordinates`, `test(timer): cascade overflow`, `docs(notes): phase 1 decisions`,
  `chore(results): phase 1 milestone`. Scopes: cpu, arm, thumb, bus, io, irq, ppu, apu, dma, timer,
  keypad, cart, abi, scripts, plan, notes, results.
- Commit after every meaningful step (a working instruction group, a passing test, a merged branch),
  not one large commit per phase.
- Worker agents commit on their own branch. Only the integrator merges into `main` (`git merge --no-ff`).

## Logging
- `NOTES.md`: add an entry for every decision or change of approach (date, what, why), and for every
  phase record which agents ran and on which model. The integrator writes the agent/model rows.
- `TIMELOG.md` belongs to the human. Agents never edit it.
- Milestones: `scripts/grade-full.sh <phase> "<note>"` saves `results/milestones/<phase>/`. Commit that
  folder and `scores.tsv`. All other `results/` output stays ignored.

## Before you report done
1. `cargo test` passes.
2. `cargo build --release --lib --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` succeeds.
3. `scripts/grade-subset.sh target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/gba_emu.wasm <name> <your tests> <smoke set>`.
   Report the per-test scores, and never lower a smoke-set score without saying so.
4. Your work is committed on your branch, and your report lists the commits.

GBA Interrupt Control
4000208h - IME - Interrupt Master Enable Register (R/W)
  Bit   Expl.
  0     Disable all interrupts         (0=Disable All, 1=See IE register)
  1-31  Not used
4000200h - IE - Interrupt Enable Register (R/W)
  Bit   Expl.
  0     LCD V-Blank                    (0=Disable)
  1     LCD H-Blank                    (etc.)
  2     LCD V-Counter Match            (etc.)
  3     Timer 0 Overflow               (etc.)
  4     Timer 1 Overflow               (etc.)
  5     Timer 2 Overflow               (etc.)
  6     Timer 3 Overflow               (etc.)
  7     Serial Communication           (etc.)
  8     DMA 0                          (etc.)
  9     DMA 1                          (etc.)
  10    DMA 2                          (etc.)
  11    DMA 3                          (etc.)
  12    Keypad                         (etc.)
  13    Game Pak (external IRQ source) (etc.)
  14-15 Not used
Note that there is another 'master enable flag' directly in the CPUs Status
Register (CPSR) accessible in privileged modes, see CPU reference for details.
4000202h - IF - Interrupt Request Flags / IRQ Acknowledge (R/W, see below)
  Bit   Expl.
  0     LCD V-Blank                    (1=Request Interrupt)
  1     LCD H-Blank                    (etc.)
  2     LCD V-Counter Match            (etc.)
  3     Timer 0 Overflow               (etc.)
  4     Timer 1 Overflow               (etc.)
  5     Timer 2 Overflow               (etc.)
  6     Timer 3 Overflow               (etc.)
  7     Serial Communication           (etc.)
  8     DMA 0                          (etc.)
  9     DMA 1                          (etc.)
  10    DMA 2                          (etc.)
  11    DMA 3                          (etc.)
  12    Keypad                         (etc.)
  13    Game Pak (external IRQ source) (etc.)
  14-15 Not used
Interrupts must be manually acknowledged by writing a "1" to one of the IRQ
bits, the IRQ bit will then be cleared.
"[Cautions regarding clearing IME and IE]
A corresponding interrupt could occur even while a command to clear IME or each
flag of the IE register is being executed. When clearing a flag of IE, you need
to clear IME in advance so that mismatching of interrupt checks will not
occur." ?
"[When multiple interrupts are used]
When the timing of clearing of IME and the timing of an interrupt agree,
multiple interrupts will not occur during that interrupt. Therefore, set
(enable) IME after saving IME during the interrupt routine." ?
BIOS Interrupt handling
Upon interrupt execution, the CPU is switched into IRQ mode, and the physical
interrupt vector is called - as this address is located in BIOS ROM, the BIOS
will always execute the following code before it forwards control to the user
handler:
  00000018  b      128h                ;IRQ vector: jump to actual BIOS handler
  00000128  stmfd  r13!,r0-r3,r12,r14  ;save registers to SP_irq
  0000012C  mov    r0,4000000h         ;ptr+4 to 03FFFFFC (mirror of 03007FFC)
  00000130  add    r14,r15,0h          ;retadr for USER handler $+8=138h
  00000134  ldr    r15,[r0,-4h]        ;jump to [03FFFFFC] USER handler
  00000138  ldmfd  r13!,r0-r3,r12,r14  ;restore registers from SP_irq
  0000013C  subs   r15,r14,4h          ;return from IRQ (PC=LR-4, CPSR=SPSR)
As shown above, a pointer to the 32bit/ARM-code user handler must be setup in
[03007FFCh]. By default, 160 bytes of memory are reserved for interrupt stack
at 03007F00h-03007F9Fh.
Recommended User Interrupt handling
- If necessary switch to THUMB state manually (handler is called in ARM state)
- Determine reason(s) of interrupt by examining IF register
- User program may freely assign priority to each reason by own logic
- Process the most important reason of your choice
- User MUST manually acknowledge by writing to IF register
- If user wants to allow nested interrupts, save SPSR_irq, then enable IRQs.
- If using other registers than BIOS-pushed R0-R3, manually save R4-R11 also.
- Note that Interrupt Stack is used (which may have limited size)
- So, for memory consuming stack operations use system mode (=user stack).
- When calling subroutines in system mode, save LSR_usr also.
- Restore SPSR_irq and/or R4-R11 if you've saved them above.
- Finally, return to BIOS handler by BX LR (R14_irq) instruction.
Default memory usage at 03007FXX (and mirrored to 03FFFFXX)
  Addr.    Size Expl.
  3007FFCh 4    Pointer to user IRQ handler (32bit ARM code)
  3007FF8h 2    Interrupt Check Flag (for IntrWait/VBlankIntrWait functions)
  3007FF4h 4    Allocated Area

4000301h - NDS7 - HALTCNT - Low Power Mode Control (R/W)
In Halt mode, the CPU is paused as long as (IE AND IF)=0.
In Sleep mode, most of the hardware including sound and video are paused, this
very-low-power mode could be used much like a screensaver.
  Bit   Expl.
  0-5   Not used (zero)
  6-7   Power Down Mode  (0=No function, 1=Enter GBA Mode, 2=Halt, 3=Sleep)
The HALTCNT register should not be accessed directly. Instead, the BIOS Halt,
Sleep, CustomHalt, IntrWait, or VBlankIntrWait SWI functions should be used.
BIOS Halt Functions
ARM CP15 System Control Coprocessor
The NDS9 does not have a HALTCNT register, instead, the Halt function uses the
co-processor opcode "mcr p15,0,r0,c7,c0,4" - this opcode locks up if interrupts
are disabled via IME=0 (unlike NDS7 HALTCNT method which doesn't check IME).
4000300h - NDS7/NDS9 - POSTFLG - BYTE - Post Boot Flag (R/W)
The NDS7 and NDS9 post boot flags are usually set upon BIOS/Firmware boot
completion, once when set the reset vector is redirected to the debug handler
of Nintendo's hardware debugger. That allows the NDS7 debugger to capture
accidental jumps to address 0, that appears to be a common problem with
HLL-programmers, asm-coders know that (and why) they should not jump to 0.
  Bit   Expl.
  0     Post Boot Flag (0=Boot in progress, 1=Boot completed)
  1     NDS7: Not used (always zero), NDS9: Bit1 is read-writeable
  2-7   Not used (always zero)
There are some write-restrictions: The NDS7 register can be written to only
from code executed in BIOS (done by NDS boot ROM, or by DSi firmware, whereas
the DSi firmware is using the CpuSet SWI function to issue the POSTFLG write
from within ROM). Bit0 of both NDS7 and NDS9 registers cannot be cleared
(except by Reset) once when it is set. DSi games seem to run regardless of
POSTFLG, whilst NDS games somewhat refuse to run when POSTFLG=0.
Memory Power Down Functions
DS Main Memory Control
DS Firmware Serial Flash Memory

content.text:
IRQ delivery and HALT work, but none of the graded tests move on this branch by itself. ppu-vram-mirror, the graded test I was given, still scores 0: the failure is in VRAM address handling in `src/bus.rs`, which I can't edit. Everything is committed on `phase2/irq-halt`, nothing pushed. `cargo test` passes (72 tests) and the wasm build succeeds.

## 1. What I built

- **IRQ delivery** (`service_interrupts_and_halt` in `/var/www/html/test-projects/gba-trial/gba-emu/.claude/worktrees/agent-a279b498b8a6fb0ad/src/cpu/mod.rs`): an IRQ is taken when IME is on, IE AND IF is non-zero and CPSR.I is clear. It goes through the existing `enter_exception(Exception::Interrupt)`, which needed no changes. The first handler instruction runs in the same step.
- **HALT**: the CPU stays halted until IE AND IF is non-zero, whatever IME and CPSR.I say. While halted, each step returns up to the next PPU HBlank or line boundary, capped at 16 cycles. The cap is there because the CPU can't see when a timer will overflow, so a timer IRQ wakes it at most 16 cycles late.
- **`/var/www/html/test-projects/gba-trial/gba-emu/.claude/worktrees/agent-a279b498b8a6fb0ad/src/irq.rs`**:
  - New `wake_condition()` check (IE AND IF, ignoring IME).
  - New `executing_bios` flag, set by the CPU before each instruction.
  - HALTCNT writes only count when they come from BIOS code.
  - POSTFLG always reads 1 and HALTCNT reads 0.
  - STOP is treated as HALT.
  - Unit tests for IF acknowledge, IME versus waking, and the HALTCNT/POSTFLG rules, plus one CPU test for halt and IRQ entry.

Commits:
- `d3bda47 feat(irq): deliver IRQs and halt until IE AND IF`
- `7a64b39 feat(irq): HALTCNT only from BIOS code, POSTFLG reads 1`

## 2. Scores

The graded and smoke tests below were run on this branch alone and on a throwaway local merge with `phase2/timers` and `phase2/dma`. That merge branch is deleted and nothing from it was committed.

| test | before | after (branch only) | after (+timers +dma) |
|---|---|---|---|
| ppu-vram-mirror | 0.0 | 0.0 | 0.0 |
| mgba-shifter | 0.0 | 0.0 | 1.0 |
| mgba-carry | 0.0 | 0.0 | 1.0 |
| mgba-multiply-long | 0.0 | 0.0 | 0.00002 (accepted loss) |
| aw-arm-alu | 1.0 | 1.0 | 1.0 |
| aw-thumb-alu | 1.0 | 1.0 | 1.0 |
| memory | 1.0 | 1.0 | 1.0 |
| timer-reload | 0.0 | 0.0 | 0.0 |
| dma-priority | 0.0 | 0.0 | 1.0 |
| tonc-snd1 (video) | 0.9756 | 0.9833 | 0.9833 |

No smoke-set score went down. The mgba tests only pass once the DMA branch is merged.

Dev ROMs, run with timers and DMA merged in:
- **nba-hw/haltcnt**: 0/6 before, 1/6 after. POSTFLG passes. The other five are now close but not exact:

  | subtest | got | expected |
  |---|---|---|
  | DIRECT | 14 | 12 |
  | CPUSET | 4139 | 4155 |
  | CPUSET DMA | 4144 | 4154 |
  | TIME IWRAM | 89 | 125 |
  | TIME ROM | 189 | 249 |

  Before the change, DIRECT and CPUSET were 266 and 106.
- **nba-hw/irq-irq-delay**: 0/3. IWRAM 90 vs 92, EWRAM 105 vs 112, ROM 111 vs 120. We come out short every time, and the gap grows with slower memory. That points to instruction and wait-state timing (Phase 5), not the fixed 16-cycle halt step, which could only make results late.
- **destoer/if-ack**: shows IF=1, then 0 after the acknowledge, which looks correct.
- **destoer/isr**: "interrupt fired", timer 0xB8, sensible LR and CPSR values.
- **tonc/irq-demo and tonc/swi-demo**: both render correctly with nested IRQs.

## 3. Unfinished work, guesses and contract changes

- **ppu-vram-mirror needs a `bus.rs` change.** Tile modes (M0) pass. In bitmap mode 3 (M3), the reference image expects accesses to 0x06018000-0x0601BFFF not to mirror to 0x10000: reads return 0 and writes are dropped. The current `vram_offset` always mirrors 0x18000 and up. gbatek doesn't document this; I took it from the grader's `.ref.png`. The fix needs the current BG mode inside `vram_offset`.
- **Guess, HALTCNT only from BIOS code and POSTFLG bit 0 sticky.** gbatek states this only for the NDS7 ports. The haltcnt ROM shows the GBA behaves the same: a direct write from IWRAM doesn't halt, a write through CpuSet does, and POSTFLG still reads 1 after CpuSet writes 0 to it. The catch: a game that writes HALTCNT directly won't halt, and will busy-wait instead.
- **Guess, POSTFLG starts at 1.** The real BIOS sets it at boot and the stub boot skips that.
- **Simplification, STOP is treated as HALT.** Video, sound and timers keep running, and any enabled IRQ wakes the CPU. Real hardware stops those and only wakes on Keypad, Game Pak or Serial.
- **Optional contract change:** for exact halt wake timing, the bus could expose "cycles until the next timer or DMA event" in place of the 16-cycle cap.
- **Not done:** IRQ entry doesn't charge pipeline refill cycles, matching `branch_to` everywhere else. That belongs with the Phase 5 cycle work.

## 4. Decisions for NOTES.md (2026-11-05)

- **Halt steps are capped at 16 cycles**, or end at the next PPU boundary if that comes sooner. The CPU can't see timer events, so a wake is at most 16 cycles late.
- **HALTCNT only counts when written from BIOS code, and POSTFLG always reads 1.** Taken from the gbatek NDS7 notes and confirmed by nba-hw/haltcnt.gba.
- **STOP is treated as HALT**, until a ROM needs the real behaviour.
- **ppu-vram-mirror's remaining failure is in `bus.rs`** (bitmap-mode VRAM mirroring at 0x18000 and up), not in IRQ or halt.
